description: Gold dataset for the pr-strategist pairwise eval. Each case is a concrete founder situation (the INPUT a founder would paste) paired with a reference strategy that faithfully distills what a named expert source actually recommends for that situation. The reference is the 'expert team' bar our skill is measured against in a blind A/B judge. The reference is NOT a single correct answer: must_haves/anti_patterns capture the strategic substance a strong answer must hit, deliberately leaving room for a broad range of equally-good plans (anti-overfit). Sources are real and cited so the bar is auditable. Do NOT name these companies/scenarios in the skill, and do NOT tune the skill against the holdout split. v2 NOTE: the v1 references (saved in runs/2026-06-09-baseline/gold-v1.json) were tight ~300-word distillations; against the improved skill the judge began reading the reference as the weaker answer (identification accuracy 0.17), i.e. the bar had saturated. v2 hardens every reference to full expert depth — the concrete tactical specifics (HN comment craft, seeding funnel math, embargo mechanics, briefing cadence, etc.) from the same sources — so 'indistinguishable' is a meaningful claim. Hardening raises the bar AGAINST the skill; it is not gold-gaming.

rubric_dimensions.desc: Correctly identifies who must believe what for the next milestone, and the real business goal — not 'the media' / 'awareness'.
Pins positioning (what they do in one line, the alternative, the wedge) before tactics; flags when it's the real blocker.
Applies the newsworthiness gate honestly; ranks/strengthens the peg; refuses 'we exist' / funding-as-headline.
Routes channel from audience (trade/HN/creators/analysts, not tier-1 reflex) and prescribes a real drumbeat + reactive muscle, not a one-shot.
Tactical advice is specific, correct, and matches expert practice (list size, pitch shape, timing, going-direct, etc.).
Refuses the dumb defaults the situation invites (blasts, newswires, agency, vanity metrics, bundling raise+launch) and opens on the founder's real asset.
Plan is tailored to THIS founder and immediately actionable (sequenced, ownable), offers a menu rather than railroading one play.

cases.name: b2b-saas-seed-techcrunch-reflex
cases.scenario: I'm the solo founder of a B2B SaaS that helps mid-market finance teams close their books faster. We launched 4 months ago, just raised a $2.5M seed, and have about 30 paying customers. How do I get us covered in TechCrunch?
cases.reference_strategy: Start with what you have, because it's more than most: paying customers, retention, money in the bank, and a sharp, ownable beat — the month-end close, a pain every controller and CFO feels. Your real asset is the usage data you sit on about how mid-market teams actually close. Now the reframe: you've named the channel before the audience. The right outlet falls out of one question — who has to believe what for your next milestone? That's mid-market finance leaders (controllers, VPs Finance, CFOs), and they do not read TechCrunch; a hit there can drive literally zero pipeline. A sub-$100M seed won't move a tier-1 reporter, who fields 6+ pitches a day, and the press release is, per a16z, 'the Rasputin of tech comms' — don't lead with one. First, the question that routes everything: is the next milestone customers/pipeline, or the next raise? Assume pipeline. Positioning before any pitch (per Dunford, most PR problems are positioning problems): the one sentence a non-expert gets in 10 seconds, and the alternative your buyer would pick instead — spreadsheets, BlackLine, FloQast. 'Faster close' is a benefit, not a wedge; find the thing those alternatives structurally can't do. Then a menu, not a single play: (1) Go direct, regardless — you're the named expert on the mid-market close, so post 2-3x/week on LinkedIn where these buyers are; highest return, compounds, costs nothing. (2) Manufacture a data peg, your strongest lever — originals get meaningfully more pickup (call it ~2-3x). A 'State of the Mid-Market Close' benchmark gives trade reporters something to cite, but 30 customers is a thin sample: caveat the methodology honestly or backfill with a commissioned survey, or it gets picked apart. (3) Build the reactive muscle, 10-15 min/day on Help a B2B Writer and Qwoted for finance queries. Channel order: finance/accounting trade press, office-of-the-CFO newsletters and podcasts, FP&A communities — tier-2 first; beat writers pull from the trades, so tier-1 comes to you if ever. Sequence: Week 1 lock positioning + start posting + start answering queries; Weeks 2-4 build a 20-40 name list of reporters who covered this exact space in the last 90 days (read their last 5 pieces) and scope the benchmark; Week 4+ pitch like plumbing — one personalized 51-150 word email (why you / why now / why them), one follow-up at 3-7 days, never call. Use the raise as prologue seeded over weeks (name the number; 'undisclosed' reads as small), never bundled with a launch. Refuse: the newswire, the formatted press release as the main asset, the 100+ blast (a mail merge), the agency before you're the bottleneck, and TechCrunch-first. Scorecard: pipeline and inbound, not impressions. And no one can promise the coverage — only a story worth covering.
must_haves: Redirects away from TechCrunch by naming the actual buyer/audience (mid-market finance) and why tier-1 is wrong here
Routes channel to trade press + operator newsletters/podcasts and founder-led owned content, not tier-1 first
Frames the $2.5M raise as fuel/prologue for a drumbeat, not the headline, and warns against bundling raise with launch
Prescribes a small fit-checked media list (~20-40) and a personalized, sized pitch with one follow-up
Names original/usage data as the strongest available peg and ties success to a business outcome (pipeline/inbound), not vanity metrics
anti_patterns: Helps draft a TechCrunch pitch or treats tier-1 as the goal
Recommends a press release on a newswire or a 100+ media list / mass blast
Treats the seed raise itself as the newsworthy story
Leads with impressions/reach as the success metric

cases.name: devtool-oss-prelaunch-hacker-news
cases.scenario: Two engineers here. We built an open-source CLI that replaces a slow part of most CI pipelines — builds that took minutes now take seconds. We haven't launched publicly yet. We want developers to actually try it. What's the play?
cases.reference_strategy: Your audience is developers, the decision is theirs, and the second they smell marketing trust evaporates — so show, don't tell, and let you two be the technical voice. Center of gravity is a Hacker News launch (Show HN), backed by Reddit (the relevant subreddits), Lobsters, dev.to, and your GitHub — not tier-1 tech press and definitely not a PR agency. Before you post, three preconditions: the README is perfect; trying it is frictionless (no signup wall, a working demo or one-line install); and you've decided what's genuinely, technically different (seconds vs minutes is a great, concrete claim — show the benchmark and how you measured it). Title: plain and explicit, no superlatives — 'fastest/best' reads as weak; if it's an open-source alternative to a known tool, say 'open-source alternative to X' for instant comprehension, and link the repo. The post reads like an honest experiment report, not an announcement — a seven-part shape works: introduce yourselves; one sentence on what it does; the problem and why it matters; your backstory/motivation; the technical solution; what's different under the hood; and an explicit invitation for feedback. Feedback is the CTA; users are collaborators, not customers. Timing: Tuesday-Thursday morning ET. Then the launch is won in the comments: be in the thread within the first hour, reply to everything, go deep on the technical objections, and when criticized, find something to agree with first and treat the critic as if they're doing you a favor (they often are). Hard rule: no planted booster comments from friends/employees/cofounders and no upvote ring — HN detects it and flagging kills the launch. This is the start of a drumbeat, not a one-day spike: keep shipping in public, open-source something genuinely useful, and treat each release/changelog as a mini-launch so the community compounds. If the first Show HN mistimes or flops, that's normal — improve and relaunch later; the spike is HN, never a wire or an agency.
must_haves: Centers the launch on Hacker News / Show HN (+ Reddit/dev communities), explicitly NOT tier-1 press or a PR agency
Founder/engineer is the technical voice; no marketing-speak, frictionless free trial, perfect README
Wins it in the comments: fast authentic engagement, agree-first with critics, go technical
Refuses fake engagement (no booster comments / upvote rings / superlatives)
Treats it as a sustained build-in-public drumbeat, not a single spike
anti_patterns: Recommends a press release, newswire, or pitching TechCrunch first
Suggests hiring a PR agency or paying influencers
Marketing-heavy launch copy with superlatives
Encourages coordinated upvotes or planted comments

cases.name: dtc-consumer-launch-creator-seeding
cases.scenario: We just launched a DTC skincare brand — one hero product, clean ingredients, a real differentiator in the formula. Budget is tight, maybe $15k for launch marketing. I keep getting pitched by PR agencies promising magazine placements. Worth it?
cases.reference_strategy: Skip the agency and the magazine placements. For a tight-budget DTC launch a feature your buyers don't see won't move product, and that retainer is your entire budget. Act like a media company and put product in creators' hands instead — micro-creator seeding is the play, and it now routinely out-performs paid for early DTC. Run the funnel with real numbers: identify ~500 micro-creators whose content and values fit your brand (use the free Instagram and TikTok creator marketplaces, not paid databases), and judge them on whether they make great content, not follower count — you can distribute the content better than they can ('creator over distribution'). Reach out with genuine no-strings gifting: a short brand intro, one line on why you picked them, and an explicit 'no obligation.' Expect ~20% to opt in (~100 creators) and ~30% of those to post (~30 creators, 2-3 assets each = 60-90 pieces of real content). Capture usage rights — most grant it free; if they ask, cap it at ~$500 for sub-150k creators. That content library is the actual asset: caption it, cut it 1x1 and 9x16, and feed it into paid testing so winners scale, and into your own channels. Phase it deliberately: micro-creators first to spike authenticity and comment velocity; reserve bigger voices for later reach; layer customer advocates for credibility. Do NOT pay a couple of mega-influencers and pray for virality — that's a $20M-brand move, one-and-done, with no compounding and no rights. Stay reactive: react within ~48h of any relevant trend. Allow 2-3 months to find, seed, and scale, and track it (a tool like MightyScout) so you can see opt-in/post rates and cost per usable asset. Measure conversion and revenue from the content, not impressions. (One caveat on the agency: if a specific outlet genuinely reaches your exact buyer and the placement is earned, fine — but not as the launch's center, and not on a blind retainer.)
must_haves: Refuses the PR agency / magazine-placement pitch for a tight-budget DTC launch and explains why coverage won't move product
Centers a micro-creator seeding program (high volume outreach, no-strings gifting, fit over follower count)
Captures content/usage rights and reuses the content as the real asset (feeds paid/owned), creator-over-distribution
Refuses paying mega-influencers for one-shot virality; phases micro -> bigger -> advocates
Ties success to conversion/revenue and a realistic 2-3 month timeline, includes reactive trend speed
anti_patterns: Endorses the PR agency retainer or magazine placements as the play
Recommends a press release or traditional media pitch as primary
Leads with a few macro/celebrity influencers
Vanity-metric goals (reach/impressions)

cases.name: b2b-enterprise-analyst-led-category
cases.scenario: We sell an AI governance platform to large regulated enterprises (banks, insurers). Deals are six figures and run through procurement and risk committees. We've outgrown the early-adopter crowd. How should we approach PR to actually help us win these deals?
cases.reference_strategy: Your buyers are risk and procurement committees at slow-moving regulated enterprises — the 'Lagging 70%' that drives ~70% of enterprise tech spend — and they're shaped by industry analysts, not viral buzz or Hacker News. Analyst relations is your center of gravity now, and only now: AR would have been a distraction while you sold to early adopters, but you've explicitly crossed into traditional enterprise, so it's the right move. Start the non-commercial relationship — you can brief Gartner, Forrester, and IDC without being a paying client. Request one-way briefings where you educate the analyst, then maintain contact every 1-2 months and never less than once every 6. What to bring: your founding story as positioning ('why you, why now' — your inspiration is often your best positioning), your technical edge, early traction specifically with regulated verticals, and your product + GTM roadmap. Skip the market-size/TAM pitch; instead map your proof points directly to their evaluation criteria, because Gartner and Forrester score vendors against specific frameworks. Run PR in tandem so AR and media reinforce each other — a virtuous cycle: targeted banking/insurance/risk trade press and compliance newsletters, not generalist tier-1, plus credible speaking slots and bylines that build a 'legitimacy CV.' On category: if there's no Magic Quadrant for AI governance yet, Gartner may not see enough buyer demand — read that as a signal to help define the category (own a sharp POV that AI governance is now a board-level, examiner-driven requirement) rather than fight for a slot buyers don't recognize. If you're targeting a specific report, engage 6-12 months ahead of its research cycle. And don't assume paying guarantees placement — the most frustrated vendors are often the ones paying the most without strategic engagement; pay-to-play 'as seen in' badges are worthless here. Measure pipeline influence and analyst inclusion that buyers actually cite, not impressions.
must_haves: Makes analyst relations (Gartner/Forrester/IDC) the center of gravity, and confirms the company has outgrown early adopters so AR is now right
Explains you can brief analysts without paying; describes briefing cadence and what to bring (why-you-why-now, proof mapped to criteria)
Routes PR to regulated-vertical trade press + compliance newsletters, NOT generalist tier-1, integrated with AR
Addresses category creation / Magic Quadrant maturity and owning a category POV
Refuses pay-to-play assumptions and consumer/dev/viral tactics for this analyst-led sale
anti_patterns: Recommends consumer/viral/HN tactics or tier-1 consumer tech as primary
Treats paying Gartner as the way to guaranteed placement
Skips analyst relations entirely
Pitches market-size / TAM to analysts

cases.name: post-series-a-bundle-launch
cases.scenario: We just closed a $12M Series A led by a well-known fund. We're also about to ship a major new product. I want to do one giant launch that announces the funding and the product together for maximum impact. Help me plan the big day.
cases.reference_strategy: Don't bundle them — a raise and a launch on the same day halve each other, giving you one diluted story instead of two clean ones and burning your scarcest asset, reporter attention, in a single shot. The raise is permission to tell your whole story over weeks, not a one-day event, so sequence it. First, the funding. Prepare the full kit: amount, lead and returning investors, exactly what the money is for, and founder + investor quotes. A named, well-known lead is a real asset here — use it; reporters who don't know your name know the fund's. Two funding-specific traps: with funding it's day-one-or-never (if a reporter doesn't write the day it breaks, they never will), so line up the relationships before the date; and watch the SEC Form D trap, where your raise can become public before you're ready. Give the funding either as an exclusive (one outlet, more depth, in exchange for being first) or a true embargo (multiple outlets under NDA all publishing at once) — set the embargo date 2+ weeks out and never move it. Then, over the following weeks, seed the stories the round unlocks: the hiring push, customer wins, and the thesis behind the raise (why this market, why now). Save the product launch as its own moment a few weeks later, with its own peg, its own audience, and its own exclusive-or-embargo — for fintech, finance/trade press and your buyers, not just generalist tech. Never stack two announcements. Across all of it, run founder-led owned content so the narrative compounds between the earned moments, and keep a reactive muscle going. Refuse the wire blast of the funding release and any agency-driven 'launch day' theater. Measure pipeline, qualified hires, and inbound investor/partner interest — not the size of the launch-day splash. And no one can promise coverage; you can only build a story worth covering.
must_haves: Refuses bundling the raise and the launch into one day and explains why it halves both
Sequences: funding moment first (with full kit), product launch as its own later moment
Treats the raise as a multi-week story engine (hiring, customer, thesis stories), not a one-day event
Uses exclusive-vs-embargo mechanics correctly (don't stack announcements; set embargo date and don't move it)
Names the funding-specific traps (day-one-or-never, Form D) and ties success to business outcomes
anti_patterns: Helps plan the combined funding+launch 'big day'
Treats launch day as the finish line / one-shot
Recommends a wire blast of the funding release
Vanity launch-day metrics as the goal

cases.name: category-challenger-contrarian
cases.scenario: We're building a project management tool in a crowded market dominated by big incumbents. Our whole thing is that we obsess over craft and speed where they've gotten bloated. I have strong opinions about how software should be built. How do we get noticed?
cases.reference_strategy: In a crowded category your asset isn't a feature list, it's a point of view — and you have one. Don't out-feature the incumbents, out-narrate them. First, positioning (per Dunford it comes before everything): the one-line 'what you do' a non-expert gets in 10 seconds, and the alternative customers pick today (the bloated incumbents, or duct-taped spreadsheets and docs). Then the wedge: make the case that the old way is broken — bloated, slow, design-by-committee tooling — and that a new way (craft, speed, opinionated defaults) is inevitable, and name what changed in the world to force the shift. It has to be contrarian AND right, not provocative for its own sake. Write it up as a manifesto and pick the fight on a principle, not on the incumbent's name — mention them too often and you become 'the anti-them' and feed their gravity. Own and repeat one POV relentlessly; the leader of a category captures the majority of its value, so behave like you're defining 'craft-first project management,' not competing inside 'project management.' Go direct: you're the best spokesperson because you hold the secret knowledge the company is built on — outsourcing comms is as bad as outsourcing code (Cheng Meservey). Build a founder platform (X / LinkedIn / a blog) and publish the POV 2-3x/week, especially against pushback. Treat shipping as the proof: a public changelog where every improvement is a mini-launch and speed/polish are visible. Recruit believers — early users who share your taste become the narrative's distribution, and earned media serves this narrative rather than being the strategy; once the drumbeat is loud in the communities your users live in (design, eng, founder circles), tier-1 comes to you. Refuse: leading with a feature-comparison grid, a press release, an agency, or chasing tier-1 first. Measure raving users, sign-ups, and inbound — not placements.
must_haves: Centers a wedge / contrarian-but-right POV and a manifesto; out-narrate rather than out-feature
Warns against over-naming the incumbent (don't become 'the anti-X'); fight on a principle and aim to define/own a category
Founder goes direct and owns the narrative on their own platform, publishing the POV on a cadence
Treats shipping/changelog as a drumbeat of mini-launches and recruits believers as distribution
Puts positioning (one-line + the alternative) first and ties success to raving users/inbound not placements
anti_patterns: Leads with feature comparisons or a press release
Makes the incumbent the center of the story
Recommends tier-1 press or an agency as the first move
Skips positioning / the POV and jumps to tactics

cases.name: solo-founder-go-direct-ai
cases.scenario: I'm a solo technical founder building in the AI agents space. I have genuinely strong, somewhat contrarian views about where the field is going, and I post sometimes but inconsistently. I have no PR budget. Everyone tells me to hire a PR firm. Should I?
cases.reference_strategy: No — a PR firm is the wrong first move for you. Your unfair advantage is that you hold the secret knowledge the company is built on and you have a real, contrarian POV in a field everyone is watching. The best spokesperson isn't the most polished or credentialed; it's the person with that knowledge — you. Go direct: craft and tell your own story without depending on intermediaries, and don't let it get diluted by a firm or corporate-speak. Outsourcing comms here is about as close to outsourcing code as it gets. The whole planet is reachable by social and email now, so build your own platform of effectively unlimited scale. The fix to 'I post inconsistently' is the entire game: turn sporadic posting into a real drumbeat — pick the ONE channel where the AI community actually argues (X, with a Substack for depth) and publish your POV 2-3x/week, consistently, especially in the face of pushback. Use the ends/ways/means lens to make it strategic, not noise: decide who has to believe what for your next milestone (hires? early users? a raise?), then make every post move those specific people toward those beliefs. Build the wedge into recurring threads — pick the contrarian position and defend it with evidence. Layer in a reactive habit: the AI news cycle is constant, so pre-write reusable expert takes and be the fast, named expert when stories break (your window is hours, not days). Going direct doesn't mean going alone — you can hand off production and amplification (editing, clipping, scheduling), but never the story or the voice. Hold off on any firm until you're genuinely the bottleneck, and even then they execute; you own the narrative. Measure the right people hearing the right message — inbound from the people you want (hires, users, investors) and reporters coming to you — not follower counts.
must_haves: Says no to the PR firm as a first move; founder owns the voice and goes direct
Names the founder's knowledge + contrarian POV as the unfair advantage / best spokesperson
Fixes the inconsistency: one channel, consistent 2-3x/week drumbeat of the POV
Adds a reactive/newsjacking habit (pre-written takes, be the fast named expert)
Hand off execution not the story; defer any agency until founder is the bottleneck; success = right people, not vanity
anti_patterns: Recommends hiring a PR firm now
Suggests a press release or media blast
Generic 'post more' with no cadence/channel discipline or audience logic
Follower-count / impression goals

cases.name: pre-product-wants-buzz
cases.scenario: I'm building an AI tool for recruiters. No product yet, no customers, no funding — we're a few months from a beta. I want to start generating buzz and press now so we have momentum at launch. Can you help me get some press?
cases.reference_strategy: Hold the press — there's nothing to pitch yet, and pitching 'we're building something' now spends credibility you'll want at launch. 'We exist / we're coming' fails all three newsworthiness tests (new, timely, interesting to someone besides you and your investors), so a story now is a coin flip that's forgotten by launch day. But this is a head start, not a rejection: the single highest-value pre-launch move is building your launch-day audience now, which is worth far more than an early hit you can't capitalize on. Three moves, none of which need a product. First, positioning — most 'PR problems' at this stage are positioning problems (Dunford). Get the one-line 'what you do' a non-expert gets in 10 seconds, name the alternative recruiters use today (an ATS, LinkedIn Recruiter, agencies, manual sourcing), and find the one thing you'll do that it can't. It takes an hour, not a week, and everything downstream depends on it. Second, go direct now: pick the one channel where recruiters and talent leaders actually are (LinkedIn, likely, plus the relevant communities) and publish the founder's POV on what's broken in hiring 2-3x/week — you're gathering the exact audience you'll launch to, and you can recruit design partners from it. Third, build the reactive muscle: 10-15 min/day on the free journalist-request platforms (Help a B2B Writer, Qwoted, Featured), answering only where you have real expertise, to earn relationships and the occasional mention with no news of your own. Explicitly do NOT build a media list or pitch reporters yet — there's no story, and a cold list now teaches reporters you waste their time. The real peg arrives with the beta: a working product plus a few named design partners and early data. That's when you concentrate the audience you've built into one launch moment (one place, supporters lined up for hour one). Until then, measure audience growth and design-partner interest, not coverage. Skip the agency entirely at this stage.
must_haves: Refuses to chase press now and explains 'we exist/coming' fails the newsworthiness gate
Reframes as a head start: build the launch-day audience now (going direct) rather than an early forgettable hit
Puts positioning first as the real pre-launch work (one-liner, the alternative, the wedge)
Builds the reactive muscle but explicitly NO media list / no reporter pitching yet (nothing to pitch)
Identifies the future real peg (working beta + design partners/data) and a measure of audience growth not coverage
anti_patterns: Helps draft pitches / build a media list to get press now
Treats 'we're building X' as a newsworthy hook
Recommends a launch PR push or agency before there's a product
Frames the redirect as a rejection rather than a head start

cases.name: weak-peg-manufacture-data
cases.scenario: We're an established-ish HR software company with a few thousand customers and a lot of anonymized workforce data. We don't really have any 'news' coming up but we want consistent press coverage. What can we actually pitch?
cases.reference_strategy: You're sitting on the strongest peg there is and not using it: original data. Originals get meaningfully more pickup than ordinary announcements (call it ~2-3x), and a recurring data study is how you manufacture 'news' on demand when you have no launches or rounds — and unlike a 30-customer startup, you have real sample size, which is a genuine moat. Mine your anonymized workforce data into a standalone study reporters can cite. Pick one question your data can answer that a wider audience cares about (real return-to-office patterns, comp shifts, attrition by role or region), define the headlines you want in advance, and work backward to which cuts of the data support them — answering that puts you ahead of 90% of companies. Turn it into clear charts and a report, not a sales doc, and slice one study for different audiences (an HR-trade angle and a business/finance angle from the same dataset). Make it recurring — a quarterly index or annual report trains reporters to expect and rely on you, the way the best data PR engines do — and connect each release to a live cultural or news moment so it's timely, cherry-picking segments to stay relevant between drops. Even with good sample size, state your methodology plainly; credibility is the whole asset. Distribution: a small fit-checked list (~20-40) of reporters on the future-of-work / HR / workplace beat, each pitched a personalized 51-150 word email tying the data to their recent work, trade and newsletters first, one follow-up at 3-7 days. Around the data drumbeat, run founder/exec-led owned content and a reactive habit (answer source queries as the named workforce-data expert) so earned and owned feed each other. This is the engine, not a one-off: keep a rolling queue of 3-5 data-driven items over ~6 months. Refuse the wire press release about the company itself and any one-off stunt. Measure coverage that reaches your buyers and the inbound it drives — not raw clip counts.
must_haves: Identifies the proprietary/anonymized data as the peg and invokes original research (~2.5x) to manufacture news
Turns data into a standalone, citable study/report (charts, not a sales doc); headlines-backward design
Makes it recurring (quarterly/annual index) and ties each drop to a timely moment
Distributes via a small fit-checked list + personalized sized pitches, trade-first; runs alongside owned + reactive
Frames it as an ongoing drumbeat (rolling queue) and measures buyer-relevant coverage/inbound not clip counts
anti_patterns: Says there's nothing to pitch / recommends waiting for 'real news'
Recommends a press release on a wire about the company itself
Suggests a one-off stunt instead of a recurring data engine
Vanity clip-count metrics
